bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Monday morning, pasting the data engineer job description before the 140 applications are screened.
bundles.why: It saves me retyping must-haves from the job description, which I hate, and I can edit each one quickly.

bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Tuesday, uploading the CV batch or importing the CSV from my ATS between two interviews.
bundles.why: Without automatic reading of CVs I would be back to opening 140 files by hand, so I expect it.

bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Wednesday in a 20-minute block, going through meets/missing flags to confirm the shortlist.
bundles.why: This is the core of my week: it turns a pile of 140 into a shortlist I can confirm, and I need the reasons to defend it.

bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Thursday, sending proof requests to the shortlisted candidates and later checking their uploaded documents.
bundles.why: It makes my checking organised and I need to send the requests before Friday, but I could chase by email if I had to.

bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Friday afternoon, approving drafted feedback for the rejected candidates instead of writing 100 emails.
bundles.why: It saves time and is nice for candidates, but it is the last thing I do and I would skip it if I ran out of time.

bundles.when_i_would_meet_it: Only when my HR lead mentions the monthly numbers; I would not open it myself.
bundles.why: It does not change my daily work, it is for my boss.

proof_timing.why: Asking for documents at application is a big hurdle that would make many good candidates drop out and gives me 140 piles of documents to check, while asking only the shortlisted keeps the effort where it matters.
